Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:40: Further, it means that he comes to resolve a difficulty - for it is fitting to ask, what does he come to teach us, that silence is good, when in several verses from the words of King Solomon, peace be upon him, the matter of silence is already mentioned - "he who restrains his words is knowledgeable" (Proverbs 17:27), "therefore let your words be few" (Ecclesiastes 5:1), and many similar ones? To this he says, "not the exposition is the essential thing" - meaning, my intent in saying "I have found nothing better for the body than silence" is that I read the words of Solomon and fulfilled them - and so it is fitting for everyone who reads the words of King Solomon, peace be upon him, to fulfill them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:41: And the same applies to all matters where "not the exposition is the essential thing," and so on, but this is a key to them. And the reason is that whoever accustoms himself to silence and not uttering a word in vain, out of fear of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, who are the inwardness of the soul, being voice and speech, shall gain from this the intent in his prayer, as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Tikkunim (page 3a), that one must direct his intent, in every place and every utterance, [that] voice and speech are the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:42: And since he has trained himself in worldly matters not to utter voice and speech in vain, all the more so shall he not utter them in vain in his prayer - and therefore they established, at the end [of the Amidah], "my God, guard my tongue from evil" - and the intent, as explained above, is that one who utters a word in vain is like one who emits seed in vain, who is called "ra" - and if a person guards himself in worldly matters from uttering a word in vain, all the more so in his prayer; and if, Heaven forfend, he is blemished in his tongue, his prayer does not ascend above, for it is subdued under that side, as explained in Parashat Pekudei (page 263b), whose wording we shall copy below in chapter 13 concerning blemish.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:43: And so it brings him to humility and fear together, when he considers what we explained on the verse (Ecclesiastes 5:1), "and let not your heart be hasty to utter a word before God" - that when he considers that he stands before the blessed Name, he should not answer his own disgrace, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 38:16), "for in You, O LORD, I hope" - and this is "my soul shall be silent," and so on - and his voice shall be low, for he shall be ashamed to raise his voice before the King. And in considering always that his soul cleaves to its root, he shall strive to occupy himself with Torah and commandments for the honor of his Father and Mother and to do their will, as explained in the Tikkunim (page 146b), concerning (Exodus 20:12), "honor your father and your mother," which we copied in the Gate of Love. And he shall likewise strive not to cause any blemish, for in blemishing he blemishes the supernal roots. And this matter shall cause him to repent of all his sins, in order to purify his soul so that it cleave to its root. And it causes him to purify his thoughts, for he shall be ashamed to think something against His blessed service, because the blessed Name watches, being within him, along the lines explained. And since he cleaves to the Tree of Life, he shall be strong in trust that nothing of worldly matters shall harm him, and that he is forever watched over from above, as it is said (Psalms 33:18), "behold, the eye of the LORD is on those who fear Him," and so on. It follows that the acquisition of this measure is the root for the fulfillment of the whole Torah, since he knows it in its secret, as explained, and shall fulfill it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:44: And further, concerning the virtue of silence, what the Tanna said (Avot, chapter 3, mishnah 13), "a fence for wisdom is silence" - the explanation is that just as tithes are a fence for wealth - for in order to attain wealth one must tithe, as explained (Shabbat 119a), "you shall surely tithe" (Deuteronomy 14:22) - tithe so that you become wealthy - and so likewise the other fences mentioned in the Mishnah are along these lines - so, for a person to attain wisdom, it is impossible except through acquiring the measure of silence. And so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:21), that when a Torah scholar speaks an idle word, words of Torah go out from him in reaction - and we shall copy their wording in the next chapter. And along these lines it is possible to say the reason is that through his silence he removes himself from the actions of the six extremities, which are voice and speech, and ascends to the place of silence, which is thought, the secret of Chokhmah - as they said (Menachot 29b), "be silent, so it arose in thought."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:45: And further, concerning the reason for the matter, since a person is silent he makes himself a chariot for the place of silence, and shall merit that the secrets of Torah, which are in silence, not handed over to be revealed, be flowed to him, as they said in the Zohar several times (Parashat Emor, page 105b). And one of the forty-eight things through which Torah is acquired is minimal conversation, and so on (Avot, chapter 6, mishnah 6).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:46: And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, in the Midrash Yelamdenu, said concerning the matter of "and Miriam and Aaron spoke" (Numbers 12:1) - this is what Scripture says (Proverbs 10:19), "in the multitude of words, transgression does not cease, but he who restrains his lips is wise" - whoever restrains his lips from speaking about his fellow is wise. Rabban Gamliel said, all my days I grew up among the Sages and found nothing better for the body than silence. Our Rabbis said, two rhetoricians stood before Hadrian - one of them was teaching that speech is good, and one was teaching about silence. The one said to him, my lord, there is nothing better than speech - were it not for speech, how would brides be praised, how would there be commerce in the world, how would ships set sail on the sea? He immediately said to the one who was teaching about the goodness of silence - he immediately began to speak. The one who had been teaching about speech stood up and slapped him. The king said to him, why did you slap him? He said to him, what I taught was about speech concerning speech, and this one comes to teach my proverb about his own [i.e., about silence, using speech]. Solomon said: the Holy One, blessed be He, did not say that you should conceal your mouth and sit silent like a deaf-mute, but rather "and he who restrains his lips" from speaking about his fellow - pay attention that you not be punished. You have none greater than Aaron and Miriam - the well ascended and watered Israel by the merit of Miriam, and the clouds of glory surrounded Israel by the merit of Aaron - and since they gave their mouths permission and spoke about Moses, I did not stay silent toward them - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:47: At first glance this teaching disagrees with the words of Rabbi Yitzchak that we copied in the previous chapter, who said (Chullin 89a), "what is a person's craft in this world? Let him make himself as one silent [mute]," as it is said (Psalms 58:1), "do you indeed [speak] in silence, O mighty ones" - while this teaching says that the matter of silence is [only] "he restrains his lips from speaking about his fellow," implying that everything else, a person is permitted to lengthen his tongue concerning his affairs and his business dealings and the like.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:48: It may be said that when we examine his words precisely, that "the Holy One, blessed be He, did not say that you should conceal your mouth and sit silent like a deaf-mute, but rather 'he who restrains his lips,'" and so on, we find him a man of peace with us, and he does not disagree at all with the words of Rabbi Yitzchak.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:49: And the matter is that Midrash Yelamdenu comes to explain the verse, "in the multitude of words transgression does not cease, but he who restrains his lips is wise" - for it is impossible to explain that Solomon's words go from one extreme to the other, "in the multitude of words transgression does not cease," and "he who restrains his lips" referring to complete silence, which is the final extreme - rather, "he who restrains his lips" is the middle measure, restraining his lips from speaking about his fellow. And the word "restrains his lips" - it appears that although there is some benefit to speaking, nevertheless it is better not to speak - for Miriam intended for the sake of Heaven, to be fruitful and multiply, as we shall copy the teaching of the Sifrei below, and even so she was punished - and this is "restrains," in a place where there is [some justification] to speak. And nevertheless, reason dictates that if he is compelled to speak concerning matters of buying and selling, he should speak - and therefore it says, "the Holy One, blessed be He, did not say that you should conceal your mouth and sit silent like a deaf-mute" - lest a person say, since "in the multitude of words transgression does not cease," and the transgression certainly refers to speaking about one's fellow and the like, I shall sit like a deaf-mute so as not to come to this, and cease from dealing with people - and to this Solomon comes and says, "and he restrains his lips" from speaking about his fellow, to correct what he said at the beginning of the verse, "in the multitude of words transgression does not cease" - for this he is called "wise" [maskil], having the sense to speak where it is fitting to speak, and his intellect overpowers his inclination and prevents him from where it is not fitting to speak. And further, it is possible that he is called "maskil" because speech is in the place of the female, and above her is (Psalms 89:1), "maskil of Eitan the Ezrachite," and so on, as explained in the Sabba (Parashat Mishpatim, pages 110a-b) - and the difference between male and female is that matters depend on it in intellect, in concealment, while in the female they are in speech, meaning in revelation - and since he is called "maskil," happy is he, for he is among those of whom it is said (Daniel 12:3), "and the wise [maskilim] shall shine like the brightness of the firmament," as they elaborated in the Tikkunim in manuscript, that no secret is withheld from them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:50: And there is a third division, which is silence concerning matters where one does not speak about his fellow, such as lengthening speech in stories of kings and parables of common people, and similarly lengthening speech in what is not absolutely necessary for his business dealings - since there is no benefit in these, one need not say "restrains," as explained, but it is certainly forbidden, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 1:8), "all things are wearisome; man cannot speak [of them all]," as shall be explained below. And King Solomon, peace be upon him, mentioned this division explicitly in the verse (Proverbs 17:27), "he who restrains his words is knowledgeable" - and the pious one, of blessed memory, explained that "restrains his words" means that he has need to speak, and even so restrains himself, as we copied his wording above - and he bases this on the verse (ibid. 17:28), "even a fool who keeps silent is thought wise; he who shuts his lips is deemed understanding" - and certainly the words "keeps silent" and "shuts" cannot be explained as referring to remaining silent or shutting his lips from speaking about his fellow, for this is not mentioned in the verse, and if this were the intent, why would King Solomon, peace be upon him, repeat his words, since it was already said above, "and he restrains his lips, is wise"? Rather, certainly he comes to teach us the matter that Rabbi Akiva said in the Mishnah, "a fence for wisdom is silence" - for even in what pertains to his own needs, he must be silent - meaning that he should not prolong his speech, and a matter that appears to him to have some justification for speaking and some justification for not speaking, not being so necessary, it is better not to speak - and this is what is said in the Midrash, "a word is worth a sela, silence worth two" - and the reason is that the measure of silence is in the measure of Chokhmah, as explained, and this is (Proverbs 17:28), "a fool who keeps silent is thought wise" - for he has grasped the measure of Chokhmah, as we elaborated above in the secret of speech. But whoever prolongs his words in worldly matters holds fast to Malchut, which conducts the world, where speech is - namely, "ten measures of conversation descended to the world, nine were taken by women" (Kiddushin 49b) - and this is the aspect of the Shechinah nesting in a manner (cf. Tikkunei Zohar, page 23a) so that he not become wise.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:51: And there is an aspect of blemished speech corresponding to "Asiyah," where the husks are, such as slander, gossip, idle words, and the like - and therefore it is said (Ecclesiastes 10:8), "whoever breaches a fence, a serpent shall bite him" - for he breaches the fences of the walls of the tongue, just as the serpent forever stands among the fences and breached the fence of the world, as they explained, of blessed memory (Bamidbar Rabbah 19:2): Rabbi Shimon bar Nachmani said, they asked the serpent, why are you found among the fences? It said to them, because I breached the fence of the world. They said to it, why is your tongue on the ground? It said to them, this is what caused me, for I spoke slander against my Creator. And what slander did it speak? Rabbi Yehudah of Sichnin said in the name of Reish Lakish: the first serpent would converse like a human being - since Adam and Eve did not wish to eat from that tree, it began to speak slander against its Creator, saying to them, from this tree the Creator ate and created His world, and He commanded you not to eat from it so that you not create worlds like His. What did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He cut off its legs, and cut off its tongue so that it not converse. They asked the serpent, what pleasure do you get when you bite? It said to them, instead of asking me, ask the master of slander, as it is written (Ecclesiastes 10:11), "if the serpent bites without a charm, there is no advantage to the charmer" - what pleasure does he get when he speaks slander? They said to the serpent, why do you bite in one limb while your venom travels through all the limbs? It said to them, why do you ask me? Ask the master of slander, who speaks slander in Rome and kills in Syria - to this point, their wording. It follows that the master of the tongue is likened to the serpent in all his aspects - it follows that he descends to the place of the husks and breaches the fences of holiness and lets the external force enter, as shall be further explained in the sin of slander.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:52: And what emerges from the sum of this chapter is that guarding the tongue from everything that blemishes it is needed, whether from slander, from vulgarity, or from idle words. And we have elaborated on the virtue of silence, because since a person is distinguished, through his speech, from beasts and animals, and is made equal to the angels, it is fitting to sanctify his speech, as it is said in the Jerusalem Talmud (Berachot, chapter 9, halachah 5), "all chatter is bad except the chatter of Torah, which is good." And it further says in the Jerusalem Talmud (Berachot, chapter 1, halachah 2), Rabbi Levi said, had I been at Mount Sinai I would have asked for two mouths - for the mouth, which is fitting to speak words of Torah and praise and thanksgiving, should not speak worldly matters, all the more so if it be something blemishing.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:53: And man's mouth was created for nothing other than to occupy itself with Torah, as we read in the chapter "Chelek" (Sanhedrin 99b): Rabbi Elazar says, man was created for toil, but I do not know if for the toil of his mouth or for another toil - when it says (Proverbs 16:26), "for his mouth compels him," it must be said that the mouth was created for toil - but I still do not know if for the toil of Torah or for the toil of conversation - when it says (Joshua 1:8), "this book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth," it must be said that it was created for the toil of Torah - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:54: And one of the authors who writes on matters of piety speaks well concerning the matter of silence, and I saw fit to copy his words, in these words: and there was a story of Rabban Gamliel, who prepared a feast and told his servant to prepare several kinds of foods, and gave him money to buy the needs of the feast. The servant went and bought several tongues, and made some of them roasted and some cooked, some soft and some hard. He brought before them the cooked ones and then brought the roasted ones; he brought before them the soft ones and then brought before them the hard ones. Rabban Gamliel called the servant and said to him, what did you see, to do this - that some are hard and some are soft, and also roasted and cooked? He said to him, to let you know that everything is in the hand of the tongue - for sometimes it is good and soft, and sometimes it is evil or hard; if a person wishes, he does good with it, and if a person wishes, he does evil with it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:55: And there was a story of a certain king who had several advisors, wise, understanding, and knowledgeable men. Once the king saw that one of them, the wisest among them, was sitting silent and quiet. The king said to him, what is this, that you are so silent? He said to him, I have examined matters and found that they divide into four parts: the first entirely harmful; the second, harmful from one side and beneficial from another; the third, neither harmful nor beneficial; the fourth, entirely beneficial. The first, such as people accustomed to cursing others; the second, praising a person to receive benefit from him, and in that same praise he causes his enemy to stink, harming the one he is praising. The third, neither harmful nor beneficial, such as those accustomed to speak idle words and vain matters - how so-and-so's house was built, and how much it cost, and stories of kings and princes, and so on. The fourth, such as Torah and the Prophets, where lives depend on lives.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:56: And there are among the sages of Torah those who divide these four into five parts: one, commanded; two, to be avoided; three, despised; four, beloved; five, permitted. One, commanded - such as speaking words of Torah and fear of the Name. Two, to be avoided - such as false testimony, gossip, and vulgar speech. Three, despised - having neither transgression nor much benefit, such as speaking of what has already happened, the customs of kings, and several matters of worldly affairs. And although the sage said that in this there is neither transgression nor benefit, another sage said there is transgression in it and no benefit. Four, the beloved - this is one who speaks in praise of good deeds and condemns evil deeds, and praises the righteous so that people improve their conduct in the eyes of others and follow their ways, and condemns the wicked so that they be despised and disdained in the eyes of others, and their memory erased, and people distance themselves from them and not conduct themselves as they do. Five, the permitted - this is speech of commerce and livelihood, to speak of clothing matters, of eating and drinking, and other needs - and whoever minimizes his words even in this matter is praiseworthy. And according to the words of the sages, most worldly talk has no need to be spoken.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:57: Things that have a great prohibition to speak, such as mockery, flattery, and speaking slander - and concerning these four one should write a gate of its own for each.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:58: In several places silence is good, such as if the attribute of judgment befalls him, as Aaron did, as it is said (Leviticus 10:3), "and Aaron was silent." And if a person hears his own disgrace and does not respond, this is a great commandment and a supernal virtue, to stay silent toward those who curse him. Also, a person shall train himself to be silent in the synagogue, and this is his modesty - and this requires great alacrity, to be silent in the synagogue and refrain from speaking even words of Torah, and all the more so other things, all so that he can direct his heart to prayer. And if he sits silently among friends and listens to their words, it is good when he is silent and hears what he did not know, while when he speaks he adds no knowledge - but if he is in doubt about the words of the Sages, he should ask them, for this silence is very bad.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:59: King Solomon said (Ecclesiastes 3:7), "a time to be silent and a time to speak" - for sometimes silence is good, and sometimes speech is good. And the sage said, when you do not find a person to teach you discipline, cling to silence, lest you speak folly. Because the tongue is quick to speak, one must weigh down the tongue greatly and guard it so that it not multiply words, for a multitude of words is like a burden, and the heaviness of a multitude of words is heavier than the heaviness of much silence. If he hears that his fellow is speaking, he should stay silent until he finishes his words - and so Solomon said (Proverbs 18:13), "he who answers a matter before he hears it, it is folly and shame to him."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:60: And whoever is accustomed to silence is saved from several transgressions - from curses and blasphemies, from slander, from mockery, from lies - for when a person is cursed and blasphemed by his fellow, if he answers him he shall multiply speech against him many times over. And so the sage said, I hear evil spoken against me, and I stay silent. They said to him, why? He said to them, if I answer my accuser, I fear that I shall hear other curses harsher than the first. And he said, when the fool argues with the wise man and the wise man stays silent, it is a great answer to the fool, for the fool is more distressed by the wise man's silence than if he had answered him - and concerning this it is said (Proverbs 26:4), "do not answer a fool according to his folly." And further, a person can reveal secrets to him, since he is not accustomed to a multitude of words and shall not reveal a secret - for a person does more with his tongue than with his sword, for a person stands here and delivers his fellow, distant from him, to death, but with a sword he can only kill one near him. Therefore man was created with two ears, two eyes, and two nostrils, and one mouth, to say that he should minimize his speech.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:61: Silence is fitting for the wise, all the more so for fools (Pesachim 99a) - and "a fence for wisdom is silence." And sometimes silence is bad, as it is written (Proverbs 26:5), "answer a fool according to his folly" - concerning words of Torah, if you see that fools are casting their words upon words of Torah, answer them to correct their error. If a person sees another committing a transgression, he should protest with his hand and rebuke him - and Solomon already said (Proverbs 15:1), "a soft answer turns away wrath," and so on - therefore each person should train himself to have soft words and not be accustomed to harsh words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:62: And be careful with your tongue to guard it like the pupil of the eye, as it is said (ibid. 21:23), "he who guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from troubles." If you sit in company, it is good that they say to you "speak" [rather than that you be reproached for staying silent] - but even if they curse you, it is better that you stay silent than that you speak, and your words become a burden to them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:63: And he should be very careful not to shame a person and not to cause distress with his words. If he sits near a person who has a blemish in his body of which he is ashamed, or has a blemish in his children or wife, or a flaw in his family, he should be very careful not to speak of that blemish or that flaw, even if he is not speaking about him but about another person who has this blemish, for he will always suppose that he is being spoken about and be ashamed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:64: If a person did something shameful and turned from it and repents, one should also be careful not to speak of that matter before him, or say to him, even in jest, "how could you have done such a thing, and why were you not careful about it?" - even this you should not do, for you shame him. If a person tells you words of Torah that you already know, be silent until he finishes the matter, for perhaps he will introduce something new that you did not know at first, and also he derives pleasure from telling you the matter - and even if you know that nothing new will come to you, be silent for him until he speaks and finishes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:65: Two people who had a quarrel with each other, and afterward made peace together - neither of them should say, "you did such-and-such to me, and therefore I did such-and-such to you," even if he has no intention of returning to their dispute - for from his saying "you did such-and-such to me," his fellow will answer, on the contrary, all the fault was yours - and from this the quarrel will be aroused again, and even if the quarrel is not aroused, the one at fault will be shamed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:66: One who sits before a sage and is silent has a reward, such as when he intends to listen. And there is one who is silent and has a transgression, such as when he thinks, what shall I say before him, since he does not know how to answer me properly, he certainly knows nothing compared to me. And he should be very careful concerning what our Rabbis said (Avot, chapter 5, mishnah 7), "seven things characterize a boor and seven a sage" - a sage does not speak before one greater than him in wisdom or in number, does not interrupt his fellow's words, is not rash to answer, answers the matter [asked] and asks according to the halachah, and speaks of the first matter first and the last matter last, and concerning what he has not heard says "I have not heard," and concedes to the truth - and the opposite of these in a boor. And the sage said, whoever speaks with wisdom and understanding is like salt in a dish, and there is grace in his fitting words upon his body, like settings of gold. "The wisdom of the poor man is despised, and his words are not heeded" (Ecclesiastes 9:16) - let him go to a person whose words are heeded and put his words in his mouth to make them heard, but he himself should stay silent.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:67: The general rule of the matter is: just as a person makes a door for his entrance, and there is a time to close it and a time to open it, so he should close the doors of his mouth with the two doors of the lips and the teeth, and be very careful about opening your mouth, and guard your tongue as you would guard silver, gold, and pearls within your chamber and within your chests - and just as you make an enclosure for its enclosure, so you should do for your mouth.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:68: See how the early ones were careful about idle talk, that they would be praised for never having engaged in idle conversation all their days. And in this matter there is a great remedy for praying with intent, for most of the loss of intent in prayer comes from idle words fixed in one's heart. Also, silence is a great fence for the fear of Heaven, for it is impossible to be God-fearing with a heart that multiplies words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:69: And with this the chapter is concluded:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:1: After we spoke, in the previous chapter, of the virtue of silence, we wish now, in this chapter, to explain the matter of the four groups that do not receive the countenance of the Shechinah, all of which depend on speech, as they said, of blessed memory, in Sotah (42a): Rav Chisda said, and some say Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba, four groups do not receive the countenance of the Shechinah - the group of scoffers, the group of flatterers, the group of liars, the group of slanderers - as it is written (Psalms 5:5), "for You are not a God who desires wickedness; evil shall not sojourn with You." And in the Zohar they do not speak of these four groups together.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:2: And it appears, as a general rule, that these blemish the four letters of Adonai, and therefore do not see the countenance of the Shechinah. And in blemishing any one group, it is a blemish to the whole Name, for the four letters are all one Name. And in blemishing the Shechinah, the secret of YHVH too withdraws from the Shechinah, and it is found that he cuts the unification - and therefore he does not see the countenance of the Shechinah. And the secret of the countenance of the Shechinah we shall further explain below.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:3: And when you examine precisely, you shall find that each group blemishes one letter - the group of scoffers, the letter Alef, and the letter Yud, and so on - and therefore causes evil to himself and his soul, bringing sufferings upon him, for the reason that the supernal flow is diminished from its source, and likewise, from great heights he falls to the lowest depths in Gehinnom, and likewise his sustenance is diminished, for from there sustenance flows - "You open Your hand" (Psalms 145:16) - "Your hand [Yud-Dalet-Kaf]" (Tikkunei Zohar, page 7b) - meaning the withdrawal of His hand. The group of flatterers corresponds to Heh, because its essence is that he speaks one thing with his mouth and another with his heart, and the blemish is found in both together. The group of liars corresponds to Vav, for the Vav is the letter of truth, as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi, page 241b), concerning (Joshua 2:12), "and give me a true sign." The group of slanderers corresponds to the final Heh, and the teachings we shall write below prove this, and this is (Leviticus 14:2), "this shall be the law of the leper," and so on - and this is enough hint for the wise.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:4: And I heard in the name of the Kabbalists that corresponding to these four groups are four impure animals: the rock badger, the hare, the camel, the pig. And corresponding to these there are four husks above to raise up the deed of the sinner and punish him in Gehinnom. And I further heard that whoever sinned and was of these four groups mentioned is destined to be reincarnated in the four impure animals, each one in the animal alluded to and corresponding to him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:5: And concerning the punishment of the mocker, Rabbi Elazar said (Avodah Zarah 18b): whoever mocks, sufferings come upon him, as it is said (Isaiah 28:22), "and now, do not mock," and so on, "for I have heard a decree of destruction," and so on. Rabbah said to the Rabbis, I beg of you, do not mock, so that sufferings not come upon you. Rav Ketina said, whoever mocks, his sustenance is diminished, as it is said (Hosea 7:5), "he stretched out his hand with mockers." And Rav Ketina said, whoever mocks falls into Gehinnom, as it is said (Proverbs 21:24), "the proud, haughty one, scoffer is his name," and so on - and "wrath" [evrah] refers only to Gehinnom, as it is said (Zephaniah 1:15), "a day of wrath," and so on. Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai said, whoever mocks causes destruction to the world, as it is said (Isaiah 28:22), "and now, do not mock," and so on, "for I have heard a decree of destruction." Rabbi Elazar said, mockery is harsh, for its beginning is sufferings and its end is destruction - to this point. Behold, it is explained how much evil it causes to himself, his soul, and the whole world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:6: And the master Rabbeinu Yonah, of blessed memory, wrote in Sha'arei Teshuvah (Gate 3, letter 174) five divisions concerning the group of scoffers, in these words: mockery is harsh, for Jehu was not punished until he mocked, even though there was no deceit in his heart, as it is said (2 Kings 10:18), "and Jehu gathered all the people and said to them, Ahab served Baal a little," and so on. Mockery is harsh, for Scripture did not specify to expel anyone who commits transgressions except a scoffer, as it is said (Proverbs 22:10), "expel a scoffer, and strife shall depart." Mockery is harsh, for the punishment of the Flood generation did not come quickly until they mocked Noah, as it is said (Job 12:5), "the one at ease holds a torch in contempt," and so on - Noah was before them like a torch, and they held his words in contempt and mocked him. Mockery is harsh, for the punishment of Sodom did not come quickly until they mocked Lot, as it is said (Genesis 19:14), "and he seemed as one jesting in the eyes of his sons-in-law" - they said to him, fool, there are timbrels and flutes in the city, and you say it is being overturned! Mockery is harsh, for because of it forty-two men of Israel were killed, as it is said (2 Kings 2:23), "and young lads came out of the city and mocked him, and said to him, go up, baldhead," and so on, and it is written, "and he turned around and saw them, and cursed them in the Name of the LORD." And Sanballat and Tobiah were punished only because they mocked Israel over the building of the Temple, as it is said (Nehemiah 2:19), "and Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite heard, and they mocked us." And for whoever mocks there is no remedy for his wound, as it is said (2 Chronicles 36:16), "and they mocked the messengers of God," and so on, "until the wrath of the LORD arose," and so on. And even in the lightest of light matters, a person is not permitted to mock, as it is said (Hosea 7:5), "he stretched out his hand with mockers."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:7: And we read in Midrash Mishlei (Proverbs 9:12), "if you are wise, you are wise for yourself, and if you scoff, you alone shall bear it" - a parable of two people, one poor and one rich, and the poor one said to him, what benefit is there to a person from you? Everything you have acquired, you have acquired for yourself. So the Holy One, blessed be He, says to the wise man, although you have acquired wisdom, you have acquired it for yourself - therefore it is said, "if you are wise," and so on. Rabbi Elazar says, if you are wise in Torah, it is as though you gladden the Holy One, blessed be He, who gave it to you - as it is said, "you are wise for yourself" - for the One who gave you wisdom. "And if you scoff, you alone shall bear it" - and not others.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:8: Further, they said, of blessed memory (Megillah 25b): all mockery is forbidden except mockery of idolatry - from where do we learn this? From Elijah, of blessed memory, as it is said (1 Kings 18:27), "and it came to pass at noon, that Elijah mocked them," and so on. He said to them, the Baal you worship - does he have "siach" [a bush/complaint]? Did he perhaps create all the trees, as it is said (Genesis 2:5), "and every bush [siach] of the field"? Does he have "sig" [a border]? Did he perhaps establish all boundaries, as it is said (Deuteronomy 19:14), "you shall not move your neighbor's boundary"? Does he have "derech" [a way]? Did he perhaps split the sea for you and make a way in it, as it is said (Isaiah 43:16), "who gives a way in the sea"? "Perhaps he is asleep and will awaken" - or perhaps he revived your dead and awakens them from their sleep to the life of the World to Come? All these deeds are only the deeds of the Holy One, blessed be He - it is fitting for Him to be served and worshipped, blessed be His Name forever and ever - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:9: And concerning the essence of mockery, there are aspects to it. One of them is one who establishes himself at the corners [of the street] for idle talk and vain words, and this is called a scoffer - for they said in chapter 3 of Avot (mishnah 2), "two who sit together without words of Torah between them, this is a session of scoffers," and so on - and it says "who sit," even if they are not engaged in words of mockery, since there are no words of Torah between them it is called a session of scoffers - all the more so one occupied with idle talk, since he could occupy himself with Torah at that time and does not, he is called a scoffer.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 12:10: And the pious Rabbi Yosef Yaavetz, peace be upon him, wrote concerning the reason for the matter, and said, in these words: and the reason is that the punishment for its neglect corresponds to the greatness of its reward, as it is said (Psalms 1:1), "and in the session of scoffers he has not sat" - and they said that the proof is from the end of the verse (ibid. 1:2), "but his desire is in the Torah of the LORD" - as though it said, because his desire is in the Torah of the LORD, he has not sat in the session of scoffers, which has no Torah of the LORD in it. And to me it is a complete proof from the verse he mentioned - is there a greater mockery than one to whom they said, count gold coins for one hour, and everything you count shall be yours, and he mocks the gold coins and disdains them? So too, one idle from words of Torah, after knowing this great reward, is nothing but a true scoffer. And so the sage said (Avot, chapter 6, mishnah 2), "woe to the creatures for the insult to the Torah" - behold, he called one idle from the words of Torah an "insulter," and this is the intent here. And when the prophet Isaiah condemned the men of his generation who were idle from Torah, he called them "men of scoffing," as it is said (Isaiah 28:14), "hear the word of the LORD, you men of scoffing" - and this is a true indication concerning all these matters - to this point. And there is support for this in Tractate Sanhedrin (99a), where they said concerning "for he has despised the word of the LORD" - Rabbi Nechemiah says, whoever could occupy himself with Torah and does not, and so on.
